narrative:
The model predicted a 52% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors in your profile. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor. At 42, it sits well above the average of 37 among students who were admitted, pushing the model to expect you would pass the bar. Unfortunately, two other factors pulled more strongly in the opposite direction.

Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the second most important piece of information and worked against you. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students, signaling to the model that you may struggle to finish in the top half of your class and therefore face higher bar-exam risk. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 was the third most influential factor and also increased the predicted chance of failure; it sits substantially below the 3.23 average of admitted students.

Taken together, the model concluded that your stronger LSAT was not enough to outweigh the academic performance signals from college and the later years of law school.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring for the bar, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas the model weighed most heavily. (248 words)
